subsection: 5. Contemporary initiatives to improve access to education

notes.h: Routes into third-level education (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The normal points system can shut out students whose circumstances have held back their results. Access routes give these students another way to reach third-level courses, and extra help once they arrive.
points: HEAR (Higher Education Access Route) is a CAO route that gives reduced-points entry to Leaving Certificate school leavers from socially and economically disadvantaged backgrounds who meet set indicators, such as family income, social welfare or medical card, parental occupation and area.
Meeting the HEAR criteria does not guarantee a place, and the points reduction varies by course and year. The participating colleges run HEAR together.

Students admitted through HEAR receive support services in college once they have started their course, so they are helped to stay and succeed, not just to get in. The supports depend on the institution.

DARE (Disability Access Route to Education) is a CAO route for school leavers whose disability has affected their second-level education, such as dyslexia, autism, a sensory or physical disability, a mental health condition or a learning difficulty. It gives reduced-points entry because of the disability.

Students admitted through DARE receive ongoing support in college, such as assistive technology (equipment or software that helps them study), exam accommodations and study skills help. Students apply through the CAO with supporting documents.

Post Leaving Certificate (PLC) courses at QQI Levels 5 and 6 are a route into higher education for students who did not progress directly from second level, through the Higher Education Links Scheme. Level 7 courses in institutes of technology and technological universities are a separate route.

Springboard+ (previously Springboard) is a State-funded scheme of part-time or full-time higher education courses at Levels 6 to 9, managed by the Higher Education Authority. It is free for unemployed people and returners to the workforce and part-funded for others, to improve employability.

Other routes and supports are mature student entry, apprenticeships, the Free Fees Initiative, SUSI grants (means-tested, towards the cost of an approved course), distance learning such as the Open University, and scholarships.
notes.tip: When asked to name and give details of one initiative improving access to third level, pick one, such as HEAR, and give its target group, what it provides and the support after entry. Do not confuse HEAR (an admissions route for individual students) with DEIS (a programme for schools) or SUSI (a grant).

notes.h: Retention and inclusion in second-level schools (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Students from disadvantaged areas are more likely to fall behind or leave school early. These schemes put extra help into schools and homes so that young people stay in education and do well in it.
points: DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) is an action plan launched in 2005. It identifies primary and second-level schools in disadvantaged communities and gives them extra support, aiming to reduce early school leaving and improve attendance, attainment and progression.

DEIS supports include an improved teacher ratio in some schools, the school meals programme, enhanced book grants, literacy and numeracy supports, the Home School Community Liaison scheme, the School Completion Programme, homework clubs, after-school supports and mentoring programmes.

The School Completion Programme (SCP) is a targeted programme of local projects, run through Tusla Education Support Service, for children and young people at risk of leaving school early. It is part of DEIS and aims to reduce the number leaving early.
SCP offers homework clubs, mentoring, and after-school and holiday activities, and eases the transfer from primary to second level, so students are supported through the change of school.

The Home School Community Liaison (HSCL) scheme is school-based and also run through Tusla Education Support Service. A coordinator links the school with parents and the community to build partnership between home, school and community.
HSCL helps parents support their children's learning, for example through courses for parents and home visits, and it identifies students who need financial or learning support.

The Junior Certificate School Programme (JCSP, now often called the Junior Cycle School Programme) was introduced in 1996 for students most at risk of leaving school early. It makes Junior Cycle more accessible through short, achievable learning targets and literacy and numeracy support.
JCSP certifies the skills students attain and the subject statements they complete, so a student who might not do well in an exam still has achievement recognised in a profile.
notes.tip: DEIS is for schools in disadvantaged areas, not for individuals. HSCL is the link between home, school and community, while SCP is the set of activities that keeps students in school. When asked for schemes for students at risk of leaving, JCSP, SCP and LCA are the matches.

notes.h: Programmes and supports that keep students in school (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Not every student is best served by the standard academic course. Alternative programmes, welfare follow-up and practical and inclusion supports remove other barriers to staying in school.
points: Leaving Certificate Applied (LCA) is a two-year modular programme for students who prefer a practical or work-related approach. It has continuous assessment, practical, oral and written examinations, in four half-year sessions with credits. It ends in a certificate graded Pass, Merit or Distinction and leads to PLC courses.

The Leaving Certificate Vocational Programme (LCVP) adds vocational link modules, Preparation for the World of Work and Enterprise Education, to the Leaving Certificate. It is assessed by a portfolio and a written exam and counts for CAO points.
Transition Year gives students an extra year for maturity and career exploration before the Leaving Certificate cycle.

The Educational Welfare Service (Tusla) enforces school attendance, follows up non-attendance and supports families, under the Education (Welfare) Act 2000, so that a student who stops attending is followed up.

Financial and practical supports cut the cost of school: the Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance (Department of Social Protection), book rental schemes and grants, the School Meals Programme, school transport (including special transport), free exam fees for medical-card holders, and laptops and ICT for pupils with special needs.

Inclusion supports help students with particular needs: learning support and special education teachers, SNAs (special needs assistants), language support for English as an additional language, language assistants in Gaeltacht schools, visiting teachers, special classes and assistive technology.
Reasonable accommodations in exams (RACE) adjust how an exam is taken for students who need it, so the exam tests what they know and not their disability.
notes.tip: Exams ask for supports that improve access to second-level education: group your answer as financial (back to school allowance, BTEA), curriculum (JCSP, LCVP, LCA) and examination supports (RACE). Do not mix up LCA with LCVP.

notes.h: Second-chance training for early leavers and the unemployed (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Youthreach and VTOS give early school leavers and unemployed adults a second chance at training and qualifications, with an allowance during the course.
points: Youthreach is an integrated education, training and work experience programme for early school leavers aged 15 to 20 without qualifications. It runs for up to two years through Education and Training Boards (ETBs, which replaced VECs in 2013) in Youthreach centres, including community training workshops.
Youthreach centres are located throughout the country.
Youthreach participants get a weekly training allowance and a nationally recognised QQI award, so they gain both income and a qualification.

VTOS (Vocational Training Opportunities Scheme) offers full-time education and training courses, of up to two years, designed to meet the educational needs of unemployed adults aged 21 and over. Courses are run through ETBs and cover personal development, business and computer skills.
VTOS pays a training allowance in place of the welfare payment during the course, similar to social welfare entitlements, so unemployed people can study without losing their income.
notes.tip: Keep Youthreach (young early leavers aged 15 to 20), VTOS (unemployed adults aged 21 and over) and BTEA (welfare recipients on approved courses) apart. For a two-initiative question on second-chance education, give each one's target group, what is provided and the allowance.

notes.h: Back to education and adult learning schemes (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Adults who return to learning can use the Back to Education schemes, adult literacy courses and advocacy bodies to study and to get support.
points: The Back to Education Allowance (BTEA, Department of Social Protection) helps people getting certain social welfare payments to attend an approved full-time second-level or third-level course and keep an allowance. An annual Cost of Education Allowance add-on, introduced in Budget 2017, is available to participants with dependent children.
The Back to Education Allowance (BTEA) helps people on social welfare payments to attend approved full-time or part-time education courses.
The Back to Education Initiative (BTEI) offers part-time further education courses run by ETBs, so adults, including those with low qualifications, can study around work or family.

Community education and adult literacy schemes, run by ETBs, provide adult literacy and other community-based courses in local settings. NALA (the National Adult Literacy Agency) supports literacy and numeracy tuition.

Aontas, the Irish National Association of Adult Education, promotes the development of adult learning through advice, support, research and advocacy. SOLAS (the Further Education and Training Authority, set up in 2013) funds and coordinates further education and training through ETBs, including apprenticeships.

notes.b: Initiative questions reward a precise, well-matched answer. Choose a scheme that fits the group in the question and give its details, not a list of several.
points: For a question asking you to name and give details of one initiative, name it first, then add two or three points of detail: the target group, what is provided, who runs it and the benefit. Giving three schemes for a one-scheme question wastes time.
To evaluate a scheme, say how it helps, then give a limit: it does not reach everyone, it depends on funding, or it depends on a student's disadvantage being identified.
Match the scheme to the group: DEIS, SCP and HSCL for disadvantaged schools, JCSP, SCP and LCA for students at risk of leaving, and Youthreach, VTOS and BTEA for early school leavers.
For third-level access, use HEAR, DARE, SUSI and free fees. For adults, use BTEA, BTEI, Springboard+, community education and Aontas.
notes.tip: Past questions ask for one named initiative with details, two second-chance initiatives, or for you to evaluate two initiatives for early school leavers. Check how many schemes the question wants and answer exactly that number.

keyTerms.definition: The Higher Education Access Route, which admits students from socially disadvantaged backgrounds to third-level courses on reduced points.
The Disability Access Route to Education, which admits students with a disability to third-level courses on reduced points and provides ongoing support.
Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools, an action plan that gives extra supports to schools in disadvantaged areas.
A programme that aims to keep young people in school and reduce early school leaving.
A scheme that links schools with parents and the wider community to support pupils, particularly those who need extra help.
A two-year integrated training and education programme for young people who left school without qualifications.
The Vocational Training Opportunities Scheme, which provides courses for unemployed people over 21.
A social welfare-linked support that helps people on payments to attend approved education courses.
A process that lets applicants enter a course on reduced points or through an alternative assessment, usually because of disadvantage or disability.
The Irish National Association of Adult Education, which promotes and supports adult learning.

questions.prompt: Outline the purpose of the HEAR scheme.
questions.model: Any three, two marks each: it admits students from socially disadvantaged backgrounds who meet set criteria; entry is on reduced points; it widens participation in third-level education; students receive support services in college after they start.

questions.prompt: Discuss two contemporary initiatives that improve access to education for students at risk of educational disadvantage.
questions.model: Each initiative needs its name, its aim, how it works and an evaluation of its effect. Option one, HEAR: reduced-points entry for students from socially disadvantaged backgrounds, with college support; limited to students who meet the criteria, so it helps only some students who are disadvantaged. Option two, DEIS: an action plan for schools in disadvantaged areas with extra staffing, homework clubs, after-school supports, mentoring and school meals; evaluated by its focus on whole-school resources and by the risk that it does not reach students in non-DEIS schools. Other accepted options include the School Completion Programme, the Junior Cycle Support Programme, Youthreach, VTOS and the Home School Community Liaison scheme, each with its target group and a comment on its strengths and limitations.
